body.heading: A light with almost no heat
paragraphs: On a warm summer evening, fireflies drift through the grass blinking on and off like tiny lanterns. Their light comes from a chemical reaction inside the lantern organ at the tip of their abdomen: a molecule called luciferin reacts with oxygen, helped by an enzyme called luciferase, and the reaction gives off light instead of heat.

That is what makes firefly light so remarkable. A normal light bulb wastes most of its energy as heat; a firefly's glow is nearly all light, which is why scientists call it "cold light". Each species blinks in its own pattern — long flashes, short double-blinks, or a slow glow — and the pattern is how males and females of the same species find each other in the dark.

body.heading: Why scientists copy them
paragraphs: The firefly's chemistry is so efficient that researchers have borrowed it. Luciferase is now used in laboratories around the world as a marker: scientists attach it to genes they want to study, and when the gene switches on, the cells glow. It is how fireflies ended up helping to study cancer, infections and how cells work.

Fireflies are also a reminder to look after the dark. Bright outdoor lights and the loss of damp meadows and hedgerows make it harder for them to find each other, and their numbers are falling in many places. Turning off a garden light on a summer night is a small kindness to a very old kind of conversation.
